question: An Aurora MySQL cluster has one writer and two reader instances across three AZs. During a routine AZ maintenance event, Aurora automatically fails over to a reader in under 30 seconds by flipping the cluster endpoint's DNS to the new writer. However, the application's connection pool (using a JDBC driver with a long default DNS TTL cache) continues sending write traffic to the old instance's cached IP for several minutes, causing write failures well after Aurora reports the failover as complete. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Configure the JDBC driver/connection pool to honor a low DNS TTL (or use the Aurora-provided JDBC driver plugin that is failover-aware) and ensure connections are validated/recycled on error, so the pool re-resolves the cluster endpoint promptly after a failover instead of relying on a stale cached IP.
options.B: Increase the Aurora failover timeout so the old writer stays active longer, giving the connection pool more time to catch up.
options.C: Disable connection pooling entirely and open a brand-new TCP connection for every single query.
options.D: Switch from the cluster endpoint to directly hardcoding the writer instance's IP address in the application configuration for faster reconnects.

explanation: Why this is correct: Aurora's cluster endpoint relies on DNS to redirect traffic to the current writer after failover, but many JDBC drivers and connection pools cache resolved IPs beyond the record's TTL. The correct fix is to configure the driver/pool to respect low TTLs and validate connections (or use the AWS-provided Aurora-aware driver plugins, e.g., the MariaDB/MySQL Connector with failover awareness) so stale connections are detected and discarded immediately after a failover, minimizing the write-error window to seconds rather than minutes. Why the other options are incorrect: B) Increase the Aurora failover timeout so the old writer stays active longer, giving the connection pool more ti... Aurora failover speed is a managed characteristic, not something to be deliberately slowed down; delaying failover works against, not with, high availability goals. C) Disable connection pooling entirely and open a brand-new TCP connection for every single query. Disabling connection pooling addresses nothing about DNS caching and would severely hurt performance and database connection overhead under normal operation, which is a significant regression with no resilience benefit. D) Switch from the cluster endpoint to directly hardcoding the writer instance's IP address in the application co... Hardcoding an instance IP is the opposite of resilient design — it defeats the purpose of the cluster endpoint entirely and guarantees an outage on the next failover since the hardcoded IP will become a reader or disappear.

question: An ECS Fargate service runs behind an ALB across three Availability Zones with desired count 9 (3 tasks per AZ). A new deployment introduces a bug that causes the application to fail its ALB health check on startup. The team wants deployments to automatically detect this within minutes and roll back to the last known-good task definition without any manual intervention or a full outage of the service while the bad revision is being detected. What ECS feature should be enabled?

options.A: ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback enabled on the service, combined with the existing ALB target group health checks, so ECS automatically monitors the deployment's health, halts the rollout, and reverts to the previous task definition if new tasks fail to stabilize.

question: A legal-records company stores documents in an S3 bucket and must meet a compliance requirement that any object, once written, is durably copied to a second Region within 15 minutes at the latest (a contractual SLA), with the ability to monitor and prove compliance with that SLA for every single object. Standard S3 Cross-Region Replication in this account has historically shown replication times as long as several hours during large batch upload spikes. What should be added to meet the contractual SLA and provide auditable proof?

options.A: Enable S3 Replication Time Control (S3 RTC) on the existing CRR configuration, which replicates 99.99% of objects within 15 minutes and publishes replication metrics (including S3 Replication events and CloudWatch metrics such as OperationsPendingReplication and bytes pending) that can be used to prove SLA compliance per object.
options.B: Switch from Cross-Region Replication to Same-Region Replication, which is always faster because it avoids inter-Region network latency.
options.C: Increase the S3 bucket's default storage class to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access, which inherently replicates faster than S3 Standard.
options.D: Write a custom Lambda function triggered on every S3 PutObject event to synchronously call PutObject against the destination Region bucket before returning success to the uploader.

explanation: Why this is correct: S3 Replication Time Control is the AWS-managed feature specifically designed to provide a predictable, monitorable replication SLA — it commits to replicating 99.99% of new objects within 15 minutes and exposes per-object replication metrics and S3 Event Notifications for replication completion, which together satisfy both the time-bound SLA and the auditable proof-of-compliance requirement without any custom engineering. Why the other options are incorrect: B) Switch from Cross-Region Replication to Same-Region Replication, which is always faster because it avoids inte... Same-Region Replication does not satisfy the requirement at all, since the compliance requirement explicitly calls for a copy in a second Region for durability/disaster protection, not the same Region. C) Increase the S3 bucket's default storage class to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access, which inherently replicates f... Storage class selection (Standard vs Standard-IA) affects storage cost and retrieval characteristics, not replication speed — this has no bearing on the problem. D) Write a custom Lambda function triggered on every S3 PutObject event to synchronously call PutObject against t... A custom Lambda-based synchronous dual-write adds latency to every upload, introduces a custom failure/retry mechanism to build and maintain, and does not provide the same native, audited SLA guarantee that S3 RTC provides out of the box — significant reinvention of an existing managed feature. question: A gaming company uses DynamoDB Global Tables replicated across ap-southeast-1, us-east-1, and eu-west-1 so players worldwide get low-latency local reads and writes for their player-profile data. Two players in different Regions happen to update the same player-profile item at nearly the same time before replication completes. Which statement correctly describes how DynamoDB Global Tables resolves this conflict, and what the architect must account for in application design?

options.A: DynamoDB Global Tables automatically merges both concurrent writes field-by-field, so no data is ever lost regardless of what part of the item each writer changed.
options.B: DynamoDB Global Tables uses a 'last writer wins' reconciliation based on internal timestamps to converge all replicas to the same final value; the application must be designed to tolerate this eventual-consistency conflict model (e.g., using conditional writes or designing idempotent, mergeable updates) rather than assuming strict global write ordering.
options.C: Global Tables requires the application to manually replicate writes to every Region itself, since DynamoDB only replicates reads, not writes, across Regions.
options.D: DynamoDB Global Tables blocks the second write with a global lock until the first write has fully propagated to every Region, guaranteeing strict serializability across Regions. AWS SAA-C03 Advanced Practice Exam | Page 13

explanation: Why this is correct: Global Tables is a multi-Region, multi-active design: writes accepted in any Region are asynchronously propagated to the others, and if two writes touch the same item concurrently before propagation completes, DynamoDB applies a last-writer-wins policy determined by internal replication timestamps to converge every replica to an identical final state. Architects must design around this — using conditional writes to guard against unintended overwrites, or structuring items so concurrent updates are naturally non-conflicting (e.g., separate attributes or additive counters) — rather than assuming a global write order. Why the other options are incorrect: A) DynamoDB Global Tables automatically merges both concurrent writes field-by-field, so no data is ever lost reg... There is no automatic field-level merge; the entire item as written by the 'winning' timestamp replaces the losing write, so partial field-by-field merging is not how the conflict resolution works. C) Global Tables requires the application to manually replicate writes to every Region itself, since DynamoDB onl... Global Tables replication is fully managed by DynamoDB itself at the write level (via DynamoDB Streams under the hood) — the application never has to manually replicate writes to other Regions. D) DynamoDB Global Tables blocks the second write with a global lock until the first write has fully propagated t... There is no global locking mechanism in Global Tables — that would defeat the entire purpose of a multi-active, low-latency design and is not how the service behaves.

question: An order-processing pipeline uses SQS Standard queues to decouple an API from a fleet of worker EC2 instances via Auto Scaling. Occasionally, a small percentage of messages contain malformed JSON that causes the worker code to throw an unhandled exception every time it processes that message, and because the message is never deleted, it becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and is retried indefinitely — consuming worker capacity and delaying processing of valid messages behind it. What should be configured to resolve this without changing the worker application code?

options.A: Configure a redrive policy on the source queue with a maxReceiveCount (e.g., 5) pointing to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), so after 5 failed processing attempts the poison message is automatically moved out of the source queue for separate investigation, unblocking the pipeline.
options.B: Increase the visibility timeout to 24 hours so the malformed message is retried far less frequently.
options.C: Set the queue's message retention period to 60 seconds so malformed messages expire quickly and stop consuming worker capacity.
options.D: Delete the SQS queue and recreate it, which will automatically discard any messages that previously failed processing.

explanation: Why this is correct: A dead-letter queue with a redrive policy is the standard SQS mechanism for exactly this 'poison pill' scenario: after a message has been received (and presumably failed) maxReceiveCount times without being deleted, SQS automatically moves it to the configured DLQ, removing it from the source queue so healthy messages are no longer blocked behind it, while preserving the failed message for offline investigation — all without any change to worker code. Why the other options are incorrect: B) Increase the visibility timeout to 24 hours so the malformed message is retried far less frequently. A 24-hour visibility timeout would reduce retry frequency but the message would still eventually reappear and still requires manual intervention to actually remove it, and worse, it would also delay legitimate retries of other messages that genuinely failed due to transient issues. C) Set the queue's message retention period to 60 seconds so malformed messages expire quickly and stop consuming... A 60-second retention period would cause legitimate messages that simply haven't been processed yet (e.g., during a traffic spike or brief downstream slowdown) to be permanently deleted, causing broad data loss unrelated to the specific malformed-message problem. D) Delete the SQS queue and recreate it, which will automatically discard any messages that previously failed pro... Deleting and recreating the queue would also discard all pending valid messages, causing significant data loss and processing gaps — a drastic, unacceptable overreaction to a targeted problem. AWS SAA-C03 Advanced Practice Exam | Page 49

question: A company hosts a static marketing site on S3 with CloudFront as the primary origin, and wants an active-passive DR setup where, if the primary Region's S3 bucket/CloudFront path becomes unavailable, traffic automatically shifts within roughly a minute to a pre-built static 'sorry page' hosted in a second Region, without any manual DNS changes during the incident. What Route 53 configuration achieves this?

options.A: A Route 53 simple routing policy pointing only at the primary CloudFront distribution, relying on the operations team to manually update the record during an incident.
options.B: A Route 53 weighted routing policy with 50/50 weight split between primary and DR endpoints at all times, regardless of health.
options.C: A Route 53 geolocation routing policy that always sends European users to the DR Region and everyone else to the primary, regardless of health status.
options.D: A Route 53 failover routing policy with a primary record pointing at the CloudFront distribution and a secondary record pointing at the DR Region's endpoint, combined with a Route 53 health check on the primary that automatically fails over DNS answers to the secondary when the primary health check fails. Simple routing with manual updates directly contradicts the 'without any manual DNS changes during the incident' requirement. A static 50/50 weighted split sends traffic to the DR endpoint at all times (not just during an outage), which is not an active-passive design and doesn't 'fail over' based on health at all. question: A production Aurora MySQL 8.0 cluster serving a high-traffic e-commerce application needs to be upgraded to MySQL 8.4, which involves a significant engine version jump. The DBA team requires the ability to fully validate the new version (including running the application's read traffic against it) before cutover, and needs the actual cutover itself to involve only a fast DNS-level switch with the option to instantly revert if problems are discovered post-cutover, minimizing write-downtime to seconds rather than the hours a full logical dump/restore would take. What approach should be used?

options.A: Take a manual snapshot of the production cluster, restore it into a brand-new MySQL 8.4 cluster, run the application against it for testing, and then perform a DNS change to the new cluster's endpoint once testing completes, accepting that any writes made during the multi-hour restore/testing window are lost.

question: A three-tier VPC has private application subnets in two AZs, each routing 0.0.0.0/0 to a single NAT Gateway deployed in AZ-a to save cost. During an AZ-a network disruption, application servers in AZ-b lose all outbound internet connectivity (needed for third-party API calls) even though the AZ-b application servers themselves remain healthy and reachable internally. What is the correct resilient design, and what tradeoff does it introduce?

options.A: Configure the AZ-b private subnet's route table to point 0.0.0.0/0 at the AZ-a NAT Gateway's Elastic IP address directly instead of its ENI, which bypasses the AZ dependency.
options.B: Deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ (in AZ-a and AZ-b), and update each AZ's private subnet route table to route 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway within its own AZ; this eliminates the single point of failure but roughly doubles NAT Gateway hourly and data processing charges since each NAT Gateway is billed independently.
options.C: Keep the single NAT Gateway but add a second Elastic IP to it, which automatically provides AZ-level redundancy for a NAT Gateway.
options.D: Replace the NAT Gateway with an Internet Gateway attached directly to the private subnets, since Internet Gateways are inherently multi-AZ. AWS SAA-C03 Advanced Practice Exam | Page 15

explanation: Why this is correct: A NAT Gateway is an AZ-scoped resource — even though it has a highly available design within its AZ, it does not span AZs, so routing multiple AZs' egress traffic through a single AZ's NAT Gateway creates a cross-AZ single point of failure (and adds inter-AZ data transfer cost even in normal operation). The documented resilient pattern is one NAT Gateway per AZ, with each AZ's subnets routing to their own local NAT Gateway, so an AZ disruption only affects egress for that specific AZ — the tradeoff being roughly proportional additional NAT Gateway cost per AZ added. Why the other options are incorrect: A) Configure the AZ-b private subnet's route table to point 0.0.0.0/0 at the AZ-a NAT Gateway's Elastic IP addres... Routing to a NAT Gateway's IP directly instead of via the resource reference does not change its underlying AZ placement — the NAT Gateway resource itself is still a single AZ-scoped point of failure regardless of how it's referenced in the route table. C) Keep the single NAT Gateway but add a second Elastic IP to it, which automatically provides AZ-level redundanc... A second Elastic IP on the same NAT Gateway does not change the fact that the underlying resource is still physically located in a single AZ; it does not provide AZ-level redundancy. D) Replace the NAT Gateway with an Internet Gateway attached directly to the private subnets, since Internet Gate... Internet Gateways cannot be used for private subnet egress in this manner — private subnets by definition route outbound traffic through a NAT device, not directly through an IGW, and this option misunderstands the private subnet pattern entirely.

question: An order-processing workflow calls three downstream services in sequence (inventory check, payment charge, shipment creation), each of which occasionally experiences transient failures (network blips, brief throttling). The company wants each step to automatically retry with exponential backoff, wants the overall workflow's state (which step succeeded/failed, and why) to be visible and auditable without custom logging code, and wants a failed workflow to be resumable from the point of failure rather than restarted from scratch. Which architecture best satisfies these requirements?

options.A: Run all three steps sequentially inside a single long-running EC2 cron job with no retry logic, and have an engineer manually re-run the entire job from the beginning if any step fails.
options.B: Use an SQS Standard queue between each pair of services with no dead-letter queue or redrive policy, relying on SQS's default at-least-once delivery to eventually succeed.
options.C: Chain the three services using direct synchronous HTTP calls from a single Lambda function, wrapping each call in a try/except block with a custom sleep() based retry loop written by the team.
options.D: Orchestrate the three steps using AWS Step Functions, using its built-in Retry field (with configurable IntervalSeconds, BackoffRate, and MaxAttempts) on each state, and its Catch field to route failures to error-handling states; Step Functions natively records the full execution history (including retries and errors) in a visual, auditable state graph.

explanation: Why this is correct: Step Functions is purpose-built for exactly this kind of multi-step orchestration: its declarative Retry and Catch fields provide configurable exponential backoff per state without custom code, and every execution automatically produces a complete, visual, auditable history showing which state succeeded, failed, or retried and why — and because state (including which step last completed) is tracked by the state machine itself, a failed execution's context is fully visible and steps can be designed to resume from the point of failure rather than needing a full restart. Why the other options are incorrect: A) Run all three steps sequentially inside a single long-running EC2 cron job with no retry logic, and have an en... A cron job with no retry logic and full manual restart on any failure fails every stated requirement — no auto-retry, no auditability, and no resume-from-failure capability. AWS SAA-C03 Advanced Practice Exam | Page 51 B) Use an SQS Standard queue between each pair of services with no dead-letter queue or redrive policy, relying o... SQS alone provides message durability and at-least-once delivery, but without a DLQ/redrive policy a failing message could retry indefinitely with no auditable record of *why* the workflow step failed, and does not provide any visibility into overall multi-step execution state. C) Chain the three services using direct synchronous HTTP calls from a single Lambda function, wrapping each call... A custom retry loop inside a single Lambda invocation is fragile (Lambda has a maximum execution duration), provides no built-in visual audit trail, and mixes orchestration logic with business logic — exactly the kind of custom code the requirement asks to avoid.

question: A media-processing application runs on ECS Fargate tasks across multiple AZs, and every task in the service needs simultaneous read/write access to a shared working directory of in-progress files so any task can pick up work left behind if another task is stopped. The storage must survive individual task restarts and be accessible concurrently from many tasks across different AZs at once. Which storage option should be used?

options.A: Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) configured with a Multi-AZ mount target in each AZ the Fargate tasks run in, attached to the ECS task definition as an EFS volume, providing a shared, concurrently-accessible POSIX file system across all tasks and AZs.
options.B: Amazon S3 mounted directly as a POSIX block device using the EC2 launch type's built-in S3 file system driver.
options.C: The Fargate task's ephemeral local storage, since it persists automatically across task restarts and is accessible to all tasks in the service.
options.D: An EBS volume attached to one of the Fargate tasks, with the other tasks accessing it over the network using a custom NFS server the team builds and maintains on top of the EBS volume. AWS SAA-C03 Advanced Practice Exam | Page 16

explanation: Why this is correct: EFS is a fully managed, elastic NFS file system natively supported as an ECS/Fargate volume type, and it is specifically designed for exactly this use case: many compute resources (across multiple AZs) can mount and concurrently read/write the same file system simultaneously, and the data persists independently of any single task's lifecycle — directly satisfying 'shared,' 'concurrent, cross-AZ,' and 'survives task restarts' requirements natively, without any custom infrastructure to build or maintain. Why the other options are incorrect: B) Amazon S3 mounted directly as a POSIX block device using the EC2 launch type's built-in S3 file system driver. There is no native S3 block-device/POSIX mount capability built into ECS or EC2 in this way; S3 is an object store accessed via API calls, not a mountable POSIX file system, without a separate tool such as Mountpoint for Amazon S3, which is not what this option describes. question: During a rolling deployment behind an Application Load Balancer, some in-flight HTTP requests are being abruptly cut off mid-response whenever ECS stops an old task to replace it with a new one, causing a small but consistent spike in client-side errors on every deployment. What ALB/ECS setting should be adjusted to allow in-flight requests to complete gracefully before a task is terminated?

options.A: Decrease the ALB idle timeout to 1 second so connections close faster during deployments.
options.B: Disable target group health checks during deployments so ECS cannot detect and remove in-flight targets.
options.C: Increase the target group's deregistration delay (connection draining timeout) to a value greater than the application's longest expected request duration, so the ALB stops sending new requests to a deregistering target while allowing existing in-flight requests up to that duration to complete before the target is fully removed and the task is terminated.
options.D: Increase the ECS service's maximumPercent to 400% so four times as many tasks run simultaneously during every deployment, regardless of actual need.

explanation: Why this is correct: The deregistration delay (connection draining) setting on the ALB target group governs exactly this behavior: when a target is deregistered (e.g., because ECS is replacing the task), the ALB immediately stops routing new requests to it but keeps existing in-flight connections open for up to the configured delay, giving the application time to finish responses gracefully; ECS also waits for this draining period to elapse before actually stopping the task's container, so setting the delay comfortably above the longest expected request duration eliminates abrupt mid-response cutoffs. Why the other options are incorrect: A) Decrease the ALB idle timeout to 1 second so connections close faster during deployments. A shorter ALB idle timeout would cause connections to close even faster and more aggressively, making the mid-request cutoff problem worse, not better. B) Disable target group health checks during deployments so ECS cannot detect and remove in-flight targets. Disabling health checks would prevent ECS/ALB from correctly identifying unhealthy targets during normal operation and has no direct relationship to graceful draining of in-flight requests during a deliberate deployment-triggered stop. D) Increase the ECS service's maximumPercent to 400% so four times as many tasks run simultaneously during every ... Running more tasks simultaneously may reduce the relative impact but does not address the root cause — old tasks would still be abruptly terminated mid-request without proper draining configured, and it wastes significant compute cost for no correctness guarantee.

question: An Auto Scaling group backs a fleet of EC2 instances running a stateful batch-processing agent; when an instance is selected for termination during a scale-in event, the in-progress batch job on that instance must be allowed to finish (up to 10 minutes) and its results flushed to S3 before the instance is actually terminated, otherwise in-progress work is lost. What ASG feature should be used to achieve this graceful termination behavior?

D) A longer default cooldown period on the Auto Scaling group, which delays the next scaling activity but does no... question: A DynamoDB table storing IoT sensor readings uses a partition key of device_timestamp (a string combining device ID and the exact ISO-8601 write timestamp down to the millisecond). During a firmware rollout, thousands of devices all begin writing at nearly the exact same timestamp values in a synchronized burst every 10 seconds, causing severe ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors even though the table's overall provisioned/on-demand capacity appears to have ample headroom in aggregate. What is the root cause and correct fix?

options.A: The table's on-demand capacity mode has a hard global cap on write throughput regardless of key design, so switching to provisioned capacity mode alone will fully resolve the throttling.
options.B: DynamoDB Streams is not enabled on the table, and streams must be enabled to unlock additional write throughput.
options.C: The partition key design creates a 'hot partition' problem — because many writes cluster around the same narrow set of key values at the same instant, they are not evenly distributed across DynamoDB's underlying physical partitions; the fix is to redesign the key schema, for example using device_id as the partition key and timestamp as the sort key (or adding a random/calculated suffix to shard writes), so that write traffic is spread evenly across many partitions instead of concentrating momentarily on a narrow key range.
